title: Medical emergency occurred 'incredibly fast,' inquest told
article: An Ontario Provincial Police sergeant admitted he was surprised how quickly a traffic stop on Highway 17 turned into a race to try to save a man's life.
Sgt. Brent Turner told a coroner's inquest Monday the medical emergency occurred "incredibly fast" after he pulled over a westbound vehicle in the early afternoon of Dec. 15, 2016.
"It happened very, very fast," Turner told the five-member inquest jury looking into the circumstances of the death of John Roberts, 49.

Turner, who had been investigating a theft in the Bonfield area, was informed that a motorist had reported an erratic driver westbound on the highway about five kilometres east of the Highway 531 turn-off to Bonfield.
Turner responded to the call from a "concerned caller" who reported a vehicle travelling at speeds varying from 60 to 100 km-h and crossing the centre line.
He saw the vehicle "within two minutes" after leaving a parking lot at the corner of highways 17 and 531, then turned around and activated his lights.
The vehicle did not stop until he sounded his siren, and came to a stop about 100 metres past the intersection.
While following the vehicle, Turner said, he saw it cross the centre line twice, one to two metres at a time.
As he got out of his cruiser to approach the suspect vehicle, the driver and only occupant of the stopped vehicle also got out and started to walk to the rear of his car.
"That was not common," Turner said. "Very, very, very rarely does that happen. Maybe a dozen times in my career" that, he said, has probably involved "thousands of traffic stops."

The man, later identified as Roberts, was moving "in a fairly slow manner" and had his right hand in his parka pocket. Turner said at first he thought Roberts might have a weapon in his pocket, but obeyed Turner's instructions that he remove his hand.
Roberts, he said, told him he was getting his wallet.
When Turner asked for identification, Roberts was "fumbling excessively with his wallet" and had difficulty pulling his driver's licence out.

"He appeared lethargic, a bit confused and delayed in his responses," Turner said. "He was very focused on removing his driver's licence. He spent an excessive time retrieving his licence from his wallet."
Turner went forward to the vehicle and looked inside to make sure there was no one else in the vehicle while Roberts stood beside the cruiser, still attempting to find his driver's licence.
He said he did not smell alcohol on Roberts' breath, but had "no idea" if he was impaired by drugs, if he was tired or had a medical issue.
"Something was just not right," Roberts said.

He saw there was "a lot of garbage and wrappers" in the vehicle, but spotted a pair of scissors, a "white, powdery residue" and tin foil with burn marks on it - "clear evidence of drug consumption," Turner said.

Turner got Roberts to get into the back of the cruiser because it was "very cold out," and he wanted to get the man off the roadway. He then went back to the vehicle to confirm his earlier observations and returned to the cruiser where he placed Roberts in handcuffs and informed him he was being charged for impaired operation of a motor vehicle.
Turner said from the time he got out of his vehicle to the time he arrested Roberts was about three minutes in total.
"As soon as I advised him he was under arrest . . . he became very upset and agitated," he started to breathe heavily and "started huffing, really, really heavy breathing."
Turner thought Roberts was going to get violent and called for backup. The closest car was in Mattawa, about 150 to 20 minutes away.
Roberts then tilted his head back and "appeared to be losing consciousness," Turner said, and he immediately contacted the dispatcher to send an ambulance.
"It happened very fast," Turner said. "Incredibly fast."
Roberts, he said, "was clearly in medical distress."

Turner went back to the car, removed the keys from the ignition and locked the doors before returning to the cruiser, actions that he estimated took no more than 10 seconds, then headed west toward the city and the ambulance that was en route, but probably 15 minutes away.
He said Roberts was not responsive but was clearly breathing and sitting upright.
Nine minutes later, he said, he met up with the ambulance near Corbeil Corners, as well as another cruiser from North Bay. In those nine minutes, he said, Roberts' breathing had become very shallow.
Turner stopped the cruiser and he and another OPP officer pulled Roberts from the back of the cruiser. Roberts had stopped breathing, and the two began CPR.
Roberts was placed on a stretcher and put into the back of the ambulance, where efforts were made to get him breathing again. One paramedic administered what Turner assumed was Naloxone or Narcan.

Paramedics and police officers worked on Roberts for 30 minutes but "there were no vital signs through the whole process. The ambulance then left the scene at 3:42 p.m., arriving at the North Bay Regional Health Centre at 3:52 p.m.
Roberts was declared dead at 4:15 p.m.
Four days later, OPP Sgt. Sarah Miller and another officer conducted an inventory of the vehicle Turner had stopped.
Among the items discovered were a plastic recloseable bag with 16 fentanyl patches found above the driver's visor and $12,690 in Canadian cash in three envelopes.
The inquest will attempt to answer the who, how, when, where and by what means Roberts died and whether the manner of death was natural, accidental, suicide, homicide or undetermined.
The inquest before Dr. Steven Bodley continues Tuesday and will hear from two more witnesses.
An inquest is mandatory in deaths which occur while a person is in custody or being detained.
Jurors may make recommendations based on the evidence presented to them, however they are not required to make recommendations.
The jury is also prohibited from making any finding of legal responsibility or expressing any conclusion of law.
